records.old: In Lesson 3 we saw that the lake's pH is about 10.5, similar to bleach, which is alkaline. Reasoning: Dissolved trona (sodium sesquicarbonate, Na₃H(CO₃)₂·2H₂O) is a sodium carbonate salt that releases excess hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in water. records.old: each lasting approximately 6-7 minutes including setup and clean-up. The teacher announces each experiment with a brief context link before starting. EXPERIMENT 1 — Neutralisation (acid + base): Each group receives a test tube with 5 mL of 1 mol/L NaOH solution already coloured purple by universal indicator. Students use a dropper to add 1 mol/L HCl drop by drop, gently swirling after each drop, and record colour at every 3 drops in a results table. They observe the indicator colour moving from purple through blue and green to yellow and finally red as excess acid is added. Students record the pH range associated with each colour using their pH chart from Lesson 2. They note any temperature change by touching the outside of the test tube carefully. EXPERIMENT 2 — Acid + carbonate: Each group receives a conical flask with 10 mL of 0.5 mol/L H2SO4 and 3-4 marble chips (or a teaspoon of crushed dry eggshell as a locally available carbonate). Students observe vigorous fizzing, collect the gas by holding damp blue litmus paper at the mouth of the flask and observe it turning red (confirming CO2, which forms carbonic acid with water). They also observe the marble chips becoming smaller. Students record observations in their table. EXPERIMENT 3 — Acid + metal: Each group receives a test tube with 5 mL of 1 mol/L HCl and one 2 cm strip of magnesium ribbon. Teacher explicitly says no flames before students begin. Students drop the magnesium ribbon in and observe vigorous fizzing and heat production. They hold a glowing splint (pre-prepared by teacher) at the mouth of the test tube and observe the squeaky pop confirming hydrogen gas.
records.new: each lasting about 5 minutes including setup and clean-up (reagents pre-measured into labelled tubes before the lesson). The teacher announces each experiment with a brief context link before starting. EXPERIMENT 1 — Neutralisation (acid + base): Each group receives a test tube with 5 mL of 1 mol/L NaOH solution already coloured purple by universal indicator. Students add 4 mL of 1 mol/L HCl from a plastic syringe or small measuring cylinder, swirl, then continue drop by drop (about 20 more drops reach neutral), swirling after each drop and recording the colour after every 5 drops in a results table. They observe the indicator colour moving from purple through blue and green to yellow and finally red as excess acid is added. Students record the pH range associated with each colour using their pH chart from Lesson 2. They note any temperature change by touching the outside of the test tube carefully. EXPERIMENT 2 — Acid + carbonate: Each group receives a conical flask with 10 mL of 0.5 mol/L H2SO4 and 3-4 marble chips (or a teaspoon of crushed dry eggshell as a locally available carbonate). Students observe vigorous fizzing and pass the gas through a delivery tube into limewater (calcium hydroxide solution), which turns milky (confirming CO2); if there is no delivery tube, hold a drop of limewater on a glass rod at the mouth of the flask. They also observe the marble chips becoming smaller. Students record observations in their table. EXPERIMENT 3 — Acid + metal: Each group receives a test tube with 5 mL of 1 mol/L HCl and one 2 cm strip of magnesium ribbon. Teacher explicitly says that no student uses a flame and that only the teacher's splint is lit. Students drop the magnesium ribbon in and observe vigorous fizzing and heat production. Students stand back while the teacher holds one lit (burning) splint at the mouth of each group's test tube; the squeaky pop confirms hydrogen gas.
records.why: Two wrong gas tests and a timing problem. (1) Damp litmus at the mouth of a flask of fizzing acid turns red whatever the gas, because acid spray and HCl/H2SO4 vapour are present; the correct CO2 test is limewater turning milky. (2) A glowing splint relights oxygen; the 'squeaky pop' for hydrogen needs a lit (burning) splint, and it also contradicted the 'no flames near hydrogen' rule, so the splint is now teacher-held with safe quantities. (3) 5 mL of 1 mol/L NaOH needs 5 mmol HCl = 5 mL of 1 mol/L HCl = about 100 drops at 0.05 mL per drop, so 'record every 3 drops' (about 33 entries) could not fit in 6-7 minutes; now 4 mL added at once, then about 20 drops (1 mL), recording every 5 drops. Three experiments at about 5 minutes each (15) plus Predict 5, Explain 10, DQB 5 and Model 3 = 38 of 40 minutes (before: about 43).
records.reference: CLEAPSS Student Safety Sheets (Hydrogen; Calcium hydroxide/limewater; Sodium hydroxide; Hydrochloric acid); standard school gas tests, Royal Society of Chemistry 'Testing for gases'

(b) The scale inside the sufuria is left by hard water, which contains dissolved mineral salts. When the water evaporates or boils off, the dissolved salt is left behind as a solid scale. records.new: CuSO₄·5H₂O showed only slight mass loss, so we classify it as stable at room humidity (it effloresces only in drier air). Table salt takes in water vapour only when the air is very humid (above about 75% relative humidity, as in a Mombasa rainy season), so it is weakly hygroscopic; our dish cannot show this directly, so this part comes from outside information. (b) The scale inside the sufuria is left by hard water, which contains dissolved calcium salts (Lesson 6). When the water boils or evaporates, solid calcium carbonate is left behind. records.new: CAN releases ammonium and nitrate ions and DAP releases ammonium and phosphate ions, which plants need to make proteins and other compounds; antacids contain bases or basic salts (Mg(OH)₂ is a base; CaCO₃ is a salt that acts as a base) that neutralise excess stomach HCl; washing soda's high carbonate ion concentration softens hard water by precipitating Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions; and NaCl gritting on cold highland roads lowers the freezing point of water because the dissolved ions get in the way of water molecules joining the ice crystal

Checked formulae: DAP N2 H9 P O4 = 2 NH4+ and HPO4 2-.
records.reference: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Chapter 11 (Solutions and colligative properties: freezing point depression); FAO/IFA fertiliser product descriptions (DAP = diammonium phosphate, (NH4)2HPO4; calcium ammonium nitrate); OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Chapter 14 (bases)

records.old: CER is a structured argumentation strategy that forces students to separate observations (evidence) from interpretations (claims) and justify with chemical reasoning.
records.new: CER is a structured argumentation strategy: students state a claim (the answer to the question), support it with evidence (data and observations from our investigations), and link the two with reasoning (the science idea that explains why the evidence supports the claim).
records.why: The old wording called claims 'interpretations' and left reasoning vague. Guideline 7 defines Claim = answer, Evidence = data or observations, Reasoning = the science idea linking them.
